One interesting effect is that a node becomes perpetually responsible for any given account, so as the state root changes, you'll still ask the same node for updates to that account. Although the address hashes are randomly distributed (kind of, more on that in a sec), the *interest* in addresses is probably not. Most users will hit the ENS registry at some point, for example. This is similar to the problem of everyone being interested in the peer that's storing the state root, but at least that interest is for a limited time period. Once a node launches, it would perpetually be responsible for the same accounts (roughly). So there could be some incentive to re-roll the private key if you start hosting a "too-hot" spot of the state. Anyone can do some work to tilt the balance away from random distribution (just run a bunch of hashes on random addresses), but of course there is a cost to create those addresses, if you want to unbalance the trie. (Although it's a one-time cost that's borne indefinitely) So we would need to do some analysis on how big a slice of state a client might choose, and look at the cost of making that state 2x or 10x bigger than the others. (ie~ how much gas do you have to spend to create a bunch of addresses with the same first byte. Assuming the clients tend to split the state space into 1/256 chunks (which seems a reasonable approximation: it would mean storing less than 1G), how much gas would it take to store `1/25.6 * (total number of addresses)` in the state. This ignores storage, but the principle is the same, for when we go a bit deeper on the analysis.
